As a former psych major, I'm still a bit apprehensive about the way the term 'artificial intelligence" is used, since it seems to stress the intelligence over the artificial.  We still have no clear idea how the human mind encodes and decodes information to form various types of cognition, including intelligence. 

So when these AI entrepreneurs and money types preach to us that AGI is right around the corner any minute now and the whole fabric of society is about to change drastically, I'm skeptical. I'm sure their cliques are about to see drastic financial changes, but in my world, less so.

I can say that I too have been given specialized costly AI tools and told to use them in my legal research work. The results are echo the gist of this article. I ask (er, prompt) it a legal question and it spits out an answer and a list of references and supporting caselaw citations. Its great for giving me a general overview and, more often than not, an introduction and some direction about legal issues that I'm clueless about.  

But when I read the actual cases it cites in support - looking for the reasoning to put into an legal brief or draft oral argument, 9 times out of 10 the case doesn't help me. It can't deal with nuances, context and deeper meaning that is symbolized by the text. Its usually a case that used a phrase in a different context or to the opposite point. Statistical prediction of word units is not akin to human intelligence. Its a surface simulacrum. Its artificial.

comments.name: A town
comments.body:
The failure of the enterprise in adopting AI is often a function of listening to the media and vendor sales pitches and not doing enough research and learning. If more executives, managers, and contributors invested themselves in better understanding what modern AI is and how it works, no one would fall into these expensive time-wasting traps, and entire economies would be miles ahead. Instead, articles like this one perpetuate misconceptions and the disinformation that’s stalling good AI initiatives. 

I spend most of my work time reeducating people who share the authors experience. There’s a better way and it’s possible today. It’s counterintuitive and it isn’t even that difficult, time-consuming, or expensive compared to traditional methods. The results really are like magic when used and managed properly. We use AI to solve business problems declared “impossible” for years. 

Sadly, vendors know and exploit executives’ combination of lust for achievement and slow-and-costly solution mindset to oversell marginal solutions at excessive prices using improperly applied techniques. Thus more projects continue to fail, only setting us further back in making the gains that will propel an industry or an entire country ahead.

Achievement follows when organizations shift to a focus on learning with small projects and emphasis on culture (as others have pointed out). One good win and everything else will fall into place and the narrative in articles like these will flip.

Russia can take this as a victory and Ukraine can work towards less loftier goals such as becoming a part of the European Union, if desired. Ukraine can save face by stating it fought the good fight that prevented Russia from taking over the country completely. comments.name: Jim Cornelius
comments.body: I am curious to know what the author thinks would be a fair resolution of the war. Negotiations which allow the aggressor to retain some or even all of the territory an populations his forces now control? Does he suggest that Ukraine should surrender some of what by international agreement - agreement to which even Putin agreed - rightfully Uraine's? That would only reward Putin's aggression, and leave Ukraine permanently weakened, with a significant portion of its population consigned to live the rest of their lives under the aggressor's rule. They are just way way out of their depth, so much so that in the eyes of the Russians - and probably the Ukrainians too - they are, like Trump himself, nothing more than useful idiots. The inarticulate premise of this piece - that the United States is the world's "indispensable" power - is a lurid fantasy that is untethered to reality. The whole world is seeing a demonstration right now in Iran of American military weakness and looming strategic defeat. The sooner the American people realise just how far the United States has fallen in terms of raw power, the sooner they will get down to the serious business of restoring what they have lost. comments.body:
I was very surprised that there was an actual party with a defined platform and ideology separately identified as the Democratic Socialists of America. Let’s stop complicating matters with topical darlings of the Left and just focus on winning elections. Simplify to increase appeal. Less is more in politics.

comments.name: Nancy Brockway
comments.body: Do the analysts relying on data collected up through 2025 recognize the sea change that the first year of Trump’s son’s term has brought? comments.body:
The DSA manifesto couldn't be clearer. It calls for "workers owning the means of production" including the end of capitalism and, inevitably, state administration and control of this "worker owned" economy.

comments.name: John Bowen
comments.body:
When I first applied for my taxi license in San Diego, California, I had to submit my fingerprints to the County Sheriff's Office. (I also had to pay for those fingerprints out of my own pocket.  If I had been convicted of a violent felony, I would not have received my taxi license.

In the 90s California began requiring taxi drivers to submit to an annual drug test before they could renew their license.  (Taxi drivers must pay out of their own pockets the cost for taking those annual drug exams).

Taxi drivers must also pay annually for a business license to have the privilege of doing business in San Diego County.

To my knowledge neither Uber nor Lyft have the same vetting procedures for drivers working under their auspices.

Uber and Lyft charge less than taxis do.  If passengers want a safe ride, they get what they pay for.

comments.body: At 74.5, I find myself dressing in ways that are much more creative and, in that way, more youthful, than I did 20 or even 30 years ago. Partly because I have some money to spend on clothes, and partly because styles are more fluid these days, I dress in ways that better express myself, are much more comfortable, and, I think, are more flattering. Years ago, I went to an event featuring Itzhak Mizrahi. I asked him for advice as a 50+ year-old woman. He recommended emphasizing legs because they usually retain their shape well into aging. That's where I started. I wear leggings (organic cotton by Mate the Label) now, instead of jeans, and long t-shirts, short skirts, or dresses every day. Add to that organic cotton sports bras (Mate the Label), layered with organic cotton t-shirts, and sweaters when it gets cold, and I'm in fashion heaven ~

I usually wear jeans and t-shirts. I have ten year old suits when needed. I dress for comfort and for what looks good to me and don’t really care what others think. Many of my casual clothes, all that I now wear are from LL Bean and in very wearable condition.  I have some wide legged slacks that look silly on me. comments.name: R
comments.body:
Punk rock forever, Rick! Wear what you love, what works for your life and pursuits each day, and don’t start worrying too much now about what others think. I think anyone worth knowing will be interested in your authenticity, though it’s possible some people will be judgy you’re not a clone of someone else. Personally if I lived in NYC I’d want to be fast friends with someone like you!

The older we get the more we get to choose not to care! But yes as the NYT author responded, wear it only if it still feels you. This reminds me of SLC Punk—punk too can become a uniform, an obligation. If it feels like the past instead of your present it’s ok to change it up. 

My stepdad spoke fondly of living in England in the 80s and seeing mods and beatniks and punks who still wore exactly what they’d always worn, because there wasn’t a culture of changing who you were for each year’s styles. (Maybe actually a function of traditionally stricter social castes there? Who knows.) But it was an amazing idea to me as a budding young punk eager to yell my rebellion at the world, to at I could dress like a girly Billy Idol into my 80s, as I was sure I would want to. Now as a 40 yr old I actually wear more 50s and 60s vintage and work in a little punk but mostly tackle the system in other ways. Whatever brings you joy!! Wear it all like a rainbow each week.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body:
The e scooters, Lime Glider type of bikes and e motos here in Seattle have become a complete nuisance. As a cyclist who rides traditional bikes, dealing with folks who have no bike lane experience and plenty of throttle feels pretty sketchy most of the time. Lime (the main operator here) says that they have made strides to keep users from riding them on sidewalks, but that is plainly not evident. The bike lanes used to be a safe space to ride a bike, but now they are inundated with a majority of users traveling at least 20 mph with lots of them riding 28 mph. The e motos travel 40-60 mph, with the target user appearing to be young males not yet old enough to have a driver's license. Regardless of the laws the state has passed, this mix of conveyances all use the bike trails and sidewalks because there is no enforcement of the laws taking place. All this amounts to bikes trails feeling essentially the same as riding a bike around Seattle did before the advent of bike trails- like you're risking your life getting from point A to B.
Paris and Madrid both had the guts to just eliminate many of these things from their downtown cores, but as all things go in American life, the solution to our worst urban problems suffers from a complete lack of willingness or ability to fix them.

comments.name: jim hughes
comments.body: Any return to sanity would have to begin by acknowledging that so-called e-bikes are, in fact, motor vehicles and not bicycles.  Moving your feet in circles to activate the motor doesn't change this reality.

comments.name: Natelman
comments.body: All two-wheeled motorized vehicles need to be treated in a similar way: some form of insurance, driver’s license and head protection. Period.

comments.name: Rich
comments.body:
Why doesn't the city just enforce the traffic laws - it'd be a great place to start.  E bike riders (and all riders for that matter) should only go in the same direction as the road.  I wonder how many accidents occur because the rider is going the wrong way on a one way street or in the wrong lane.  The same holds true for bike lanes and I have to believe many bike riders would appreciate that.  Half the time you don't know what direction the bike lane is going based on the riders, even though the big arrows are evident on the street.  

Second, E bike riders should not be riding on sidewalks.  If you're on the sidewalk, you walk your bike.  Same with motorized scooters.  There should be zero tolerance to motorized vehicles on the sidewalk.

All of this sounds like common sense, but I see these violations every day.  The city could take a big step towards reform just by curbing the anarchy that currently exists.

comments.name: Mike B

comments.name: Jaybc

comments.name: Cate B.

I was lucky that I didn't have an end of the life ailment.  But I did have stage 1 lung cancer not to mention 5 spinal compression fractures from osteoporosis and I was utterly terrified.  Terrified really is the word though it doesn't begin to describe it.

What mattered most was accurate information.  Did I know what I was heading into?  Of course, not.  Did I know if I would get through this whatever it turned out to be?  Not a change.  It was a huge horrible unknown.  I will never stop being thankful for the doctors who held my hand when I was too terrified to be coherent, who who told me the truth when I was scared, who answered my questions and who coped with my horror that they couldn't necessarily predict the outcome.

I am not as sick as some of the people described.  But trust me, even a lesser version is hell.  And thankfully , 12 years later i am still here, still speaking up and still so glad I had a medical team who knew how to communicate.

The most important consequence of open weights is that you can run the model on your own computer, or for larger models rent hardware or hire a third party to run it there. If the model is closed weights, you have to send your data to the company that runs the model, and pay them to run it.

Open source models are a bit different from open source software. Open source models disclose what data they were trained on, and what the training protocol was (with sufficient detail to reproduce the process). There are very few open source models, and even fewer that exclusively use training data with the permission of the owners or creators of the data.

Let’s talk about the real costs of building massive hot, water hungry data centers in drought stricken deserts of the West. 

Did you know that birds pant when it’s 113 in the shade in the Sonoran Desert when temps hit 120 degrees in the Coachella Valley as they did this week? 

Data centers accelerate climate change with greenhouse gas emissions and create heat islands that can raise air and land temperatures by five to 16 degrees for six miles around massive data centers that expel waste heat with a total thermal output equivalent to tens of thousands of households.

What about water security? This summer, residents of the Coachella and Imperial valleys beat back wildly irresponsible schemes to build the largest data centers in the state on top of our dwindling aquifer, which is already over pumped, with 80 percent of it’s capacity recharged annually by imported water more than 200 miles from the dying Colorado River. 

We are told constantly to conserve water. But all bets are off for greedy billionaires lounging  on yachts when it comes to water security for the poorest people in the state coping with unlivable heat and existing health threats in a region plagued by toxic dust from the dying Salton Sea. 

We’ve hit our limits. No more data centers in the desert!

I think the fight against AI data centers is rooted in longstanding mistrust by many Americans of intellectuals, academics, scientists and credentialed experts in general. 

Richard Hofstadter’s 1963 Pulitzer Prize-winning book, “Anti-Intellectualism in American Life”,  identified a recurring pattern in American history: a suspicion of the "expert class" and institutional elites. When applied to the AI boom, several historical parallels emerge including the populist rejection of technological progress and the management of profits by an elite class of technocrats.

What’s curious about the rebellion against AI and data centers is the opposition by liberals and conservatives alike. Anti-intellectualism provides the cultural tinder, but the threat of rising electric bills, dried-up water tables, and job displacement is the spark blocking the data center projects. 

Whenever I suggest to liberal friends and colleagues that they can slow data center growth by not using AI and data in their personal lives and restricting data use to essential work purposes only, I’m either met with silence or the old argument that data use by one person doesn’t matter. But it does matter.

There are some parallels with the emergence of the internet in the early 2000s.  At first the internet was seen as some sort of "magic" that defied normal business disciplines.  It soon showed it could not defy business gravity.

In order to get value out of AI for a business, the process still requires similar discipline to deploying any technology.

1. Define clearly what the problems to solve, or opportunity to exploits, are, and what success should look like.

2. Specify how the new technology will achieve those expectations, as well as operate within the business.

3. Build / configure the new technology.

4. Test that it works as intended

5. Deploy it into the business, and monitor that it is doing what it is supposed to.

This process need not be a rigid waterfall, it can equally be exploratory and iterative, which can be very useful with a new technology where it takes time to understand it's possible uses.

Technology that operates and makes decisions based sophisticated models needs particular ongoing monitoring.  Having worked in the banking industry which already uses sophisticated models for decision making such as credit assessment, I have seen the significant level of effort needed to make sure its decision making is understood and can be regularly validated.

Businesses which pre-emptively get rid of much of their subject matter expertise "because AI will do it all now", risk very unfortunate consequences when AI runs amok.

When an elected official of a certain age is physically incapacitated, it becomes a matter of selfishness that he/she remains in office, on salary, while unable to travel to the chamber fulfill the demands of the job. But when the issue is cognitive, and the official is unable to render his/her own decision to retire, their entire staff must hide the nature of the problem in order to save their own jobs -- which serves them, but not the rep's constituents. 

We need some standards -- maybe a physical and mental/cognitive evaluation at the beginning of each term? (Could a psych exam have spared us George Santos?) 1) US President: 35 Years - 70 years (must be under 70 at the time they would leave office).
2) US Senator: 30 Years - 60 years.
3) US Congressperson: 25 years - 50 years.

So a 65-year old who had not previously been elected could serve at most one term as US President; while a 67-year old would be barred from running at all, although I suppose we could also allow for them to serve a partial term if the electorate would accept it.

Think of it as affirmative action for the non-aged, if that helps.

We probably also need a way for a reasonable minority in congress to have the power to summon an elected official for a wellness check and a cognitive test.

This article rightly humanizes the trapped sailors, but it leaves readers with only half the story. The Strait of Hormuz is not merely a shipping lane; it is one of the world’s most important strategic chokepoints. Control over it creates leverage over energy, trade, insurance, and diplomacy. That broader context helps explain why civilian ships become targets during conflict—and why protecting commercial shipping is about far more than economics.

Iran bears responsibility for seizing commercial vessels and using civilian crews as leverage. Yet this crisis also raises uncomfortable questions for governments, international organizations, and shipping companies. Have they done enough to protect the people whose labor keeps global commerce moving? Humanitarian concern should include not only sympathy after the fact but also serious reflection on the incentives and policies that place civilians in harm’s way.

The moral issue runs even deeper. These sailors are not bargaining chips or statistics. They are men made in the image of God, with families waiting for them. Justice requires opposing aggression and seeking their release. Mercy requires refusing to let their humanity disappear beneath geopolitical narratives. We need both compassion and context if we hope to understand this tragedy—and to reduce the likelihood of repeating it.

We arrive and there are only six other souls there, but Dudley Laufman will, nevertheless, call the dance for us diehards. The snow had started during our 50-mile drive there and it continued while we danced, and then through the drive home. Were we crazy to go? Certainly, but we had the delight of this odd evening, with Dudley on the squeeze box and his wife on a snare drum. That was all and that was enough.

comments.name: Alibet

Contra-dancing was a formative part of my childhood! I grew up in the 70's in Concord, Mass., playing for contra dances -- I remember Dudley, a true character -- in town halls, community centers and gyms. What we lose when we don't dance... 
No need to suffer the ignomies of not having brought a partner, and no need to stay with anyone for more than one dance. And no way to know, by looking at someone, whether or not they were a good dancer: an excellent broader life lesson. 
There is nothing -- and I do mean *nothing* -- more thrilling, more captivating, more joyful than moving your body, and someone else's, to live music. Vive contra dance!

comments.name: dale m

It was still a dizzying experience, and one I will never forget.  The band was a fairly well known group, and I don't know if Mr. Laufman was calling that evening, but bless him for keeping this alive.  I spent many years sharing the simplest of contras with young people preparing to be music teachers, which suggests that his influence will live on and on.

comments.body: Thanks for covering this! I am a big fan of contra and square dancing but was not familiar with Mr. Laufman. There is a robust "old time" scene, in the D.C. area, on down through Virgina and West Virginia. As Mr. Laufman noted from his own experience, there is a growing appeal with young people. As more and more of our daily experience becomes mediated by screens and now fake stuff, I'd imagine we're in for another resurgence of folk dance.

There's a square dance every night. One thing I love about that week, and about Laufman's story, is how it offers a glimpse of a vibrant tradition running outside the homogenous mainstream of American culture, with its own history -- a bit of that "Old, Weird America."

comments.name: Billy Romp
comments.body:
I spent many years playing mandolin in a busy contra dance band in Vermont. As an extrovert, I thought I would try my hand at calling. 

It looks easy. It isn't. One mistake in timing a call will send a room full of people into confused chaos. Your next dance will have half as many dancers take their place on the floor. Your next mistake might end your last chance at calling. I called a dozen dances; the stress was too much for me, so I returned to the safety of the band, where mistakes were barely noticed.

It's not an exaggeration to say that he enriched the lives of thousands of people, including my own.

The rains we are famous for start in late October and usually end by late June at the latest. July 4th fireworks maximize our anxieties, as you might imagine, as it's almost inevitably bone dry by then and the forest is fire-ready. Local open burning bans are in affect these days from June 1 until the rains return.  The question in my mind: should people setting off fireworks that then ignite forest fires be punished as arsonists?  Our family members in the Spokane area report that folks there are pulling together admirably to help their affected neighbors. We here are ready to put up displaced folks if they need that. comments.name: Doug
comments.body: "In the aftermath, some residents and business owners bristled at the sight of the intact shopping mall sitting within a residential grid blanketed in ash and rubble, the firefighters who guarded it for two more weeks."  This is nonsense.  My family lost 4 homes and everything we owned.  "Bristling" doesn't come close to the raw anger that my family, friends and I feel at the gross failure of leadership that we learned about in the wake of the fire.  Examples:  The fire hydrant 40 feel from my home was never charged with water, the covered reservoir above our community was empty, and most glaringly, the fire that destroyed our community was part 2 of a small fire that reignited because fire crews were ordered to leave the scene--replete with hot rocks and smoke coming from the ground.  This was a violation of firefighting 101.  The text messages of this tragic failure of judgment is well document in text messages.  Kudos to Mr. Caruso for having the foresight realize that gross incompetence was going to kill many people and destroy our community.  Thank you Mr. Caruso for your leadership and for putting enormous resources into restoring our town center and community.  And yes, the development has fancy stores, but it is also a community center that is used by people to just hang out, celebrate holidays, and share the delight of a great farmers market.

I am astonished that streaming sunlight into an art gallery was not a top architectural consideration from the very first day of planning,

comments.name: Mike H
comments.body:
Wyoming is right to push back on "red flag laws." These laws are Alice in Wonderland's "Sentence first—verdict afterwards," and they perfectly illustrate how the corporate gun banning lobby will stop at nothing—not even the due process protections of the Constitution—to effect their dangerous prohibitions.

That said: in the continuum of mental health decline that may ultimately result in a successful suicide, the gun falls at the end of the chain. There's a lot of upstream dominos that need to tip over first. And like all medicine, the best interventions happen earlier than later. A small but growing cadre of experts are doing excellent research on this, and even they are understanding that limiting access to gun is not a good or workable solution.

I grew up and have lived in rural communities. We are more than aware that "mental illness is real and suicides are preventable." I don't believe for a second the sweeping generalization that "much of Wyoming is not there yet." This has the tinny ring of ivy leaguers lecturing to us bumpkins.

I'd encourage everyone assuming they have "the answer" to go spend some time with these people instead of listening to them. Rural communities (like urban communities) have plenty of problems, but those bumpkins are more than smart enough to know when they're being sold a load of bunkum.

The article doesn’t share what the suicide rates are in Wyoming.

But cultural norms seem to play a large role. According to the World Population Review. The three highest suicide rates are Greenland, Suriname, and South Korea.  Three very different countries.

Greenland may be more like Wyoming—rural, isolated and many people probably have firearms.  But Suriname? South Korea? Korea would seem just the opposite—urban, social, and strict gun control.

The US by the way is about average and lower than most European countries. Japan for instance is about a third higher than the US, and again has strict gun control.

I also suspect that most skepticism about mental health therapy is based on uncertainty about its effectiveness. It gets a lot of play, but does it work? Where are the stats?

https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/suicide-rate-by-country

comments.body: Another reason to celebrate NOLA, one of the most wonderful US cities, and one of the greatest US food destinations. Dakar has received many accolades. Congratulations are in order. It is obviously a noteworthy restaurant.  Here, in this review, it gets a Very Good rating. I understand that means "Very Good" and that it's praise. Well deserved clearly because there is not one word about the food that is critical. Not one. That's excellent. The food seems without fault. That explains the James Beard awards, the ranking on North America's 50 Best, and the Michelin notice. The only fault found in the entire piece is the temporarily unfinished space, used for waiting now, that felt chilly and off-putting. So, is that the basis of the "Very Good" rating as opposed to, say, a rating of Excellent? I ask not because I'm arguing with the evaluation but because I'm trying to understand it and I'm trying to understand how exactly you assign it. Not just in this instance, but across the board. Especially, I  suppose, in a review in which the food receives nothing but fulsome praise and appreciation. I am happy for Dakar. For all the notice it has gotten. The simple answer to this is that healthcare is a public good and ought to be treated as such.  Universal health care, paid for and regulated by the government, wouldn't be a perfect system, but cutting out private insurers (other than for top-up) would eliminate the processes of private arbitration and litigation that simply increase the cost of health care without providing any benefit to the consumers of it.

But, since we consider shareholder profits and executive compensation more of a human right here than we do actual life and quality of life of all humans, we have the system we have.

comments.name: Sarah Kliff
comments.body: In 2020, I spent a lot of time covering Congress’ passage of a ban on surprise medical bills. There was one phrase I heard a lot back then: baseball-style arbitration — the same system Major League Baseball uses to settle salary disputes between players and teams. Legislators planned to mimic that system to sort out cases where doctors and insurers couldn’t agree on a price for emergency services. But applying sports logic to health care hasn't worked out as planned. My colleague Margot and I set out to figure out why.
